extracted.intended_audience: readers of Montaigne; students of literature; general educated readers interested in essayistic/autobiographical writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing intimate, autobiographical essays emphasizing private intent, sincerity of voice, and self-knowledge rather than public ornament or ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intention: private/domestic end
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have proposed to myself no other than a domestic and private end: I have had no consideration at all either to thy service or to my glory. I have dedicated it to the particular commodity of my kinsfolk and friends...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write with the aim of serving a private, specific audience (friends/kin) rather than pursuing public fame; let the work preserve traits and humours for those who knew the author. The passage stresses that modest, inward aims justify a plain, unvarnished style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and simplicity of voice; avoid borrowed beauties
rubrics_metrics.description: “Had my intention been to seek the world’s favour, I should surely have adorned myself with borrowed beauties: I desire therein to be viewed as I appear in mine own genuine, simple, and ordinary manner, without study and artifice: for it is myself I paint.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a genuine, unadorned voice over ornate, borrowed stylistic flourishes. Present yourself 'as you appear' — emphasize naturalness, minimal artifice, and an ordinary manner rather than rhetorical embellishment intended to please or impress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full honesty in self-portraiture (including defects)
rubrics_metrics.description: “My defects are therein to be read to the life... If I had lived among those nations... I would most willingly have painted myself quite fully and quite naked.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to record personal faults and imperfections with frankness; authenticity includes admitting defects rather than concealing them to flatter oneself or an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do thine own work; know thyself
rubrics_metrics.description: “Do thine own work, and know thyself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A writer (or practitioner) should focus on what is proper to their own nature and capacity: concentrate on doing your own work well rather than imitating others, refuse superfluous employments, and avoid mistaking another’s role for your own. Self-knowledge informs suitable subject matter and mode of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the present over anxious pursuit of the future
rubrics_metrics.description: “We are never present with, but always beyond ourselves: fear, desire, hope, still push us on towards the future, depriving us, in the meantime, of the sense and consideration of that which is to amuse us with the thought of what shall be...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid grounding your work in restless pursuit of future advantage or reputation; attend to present realities and present pleasures. For essayists: draw on immediate experience and present-minded reflection rather than speculative chasing of future reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject ostentation and false praise; value truthful assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: “That the language of men bred up in courts is always full of vain ostentation and false testimony, every one indifferently magnifying his own master, and stretching his commendation to the utmost extent of virtue and sovereign grandeur.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid flattery, ostentation, and false testimony in writing and criticism; prefer candid, measured, and honest appraisal over exaggerated praise intended to curry favour.
